tbl21_1: A four-column diagnostic roadmap whose seven rows each pair a symptom of a failing spectral computation (coefficients peaking at a high mode, slow algebraic coefficient decay, a slope change in the coefficient plot, a non-decaying oscillatory asymptote, expensive residual evaluations, the need for a Hilbert transform, or working symbolically at small N) with its structural clue, the recommended remedy, and the chapter section that treats it; the takeaway is that each failure mode is matched to one specific structural fix.
fig21_1: Two side-by-side panels comparing a naive and a tailored truncation length for Chebyshev collocation of sech of y at fixed N equals forty-eight. The left panel plots the bell-shaped sech pulse against y with two sets of grid markers: a naive grid for L equals thirty (coral circles) spreading most points far out where the function is essentially zero, and a tailored grid for L equals eight (teal triangles) concentrating points inside the pulse. The right panel shows pointwise error across the inner window for each: the naive case peaks near nine point six times ten to the power minus two, the tailored case near one times ten to the power minus four, a roughly thousand-fold gain from changing one constant.
fig21_2: Six panels in a three-by-two grid for Mathieu sideband truncation; top row shows coefficient pictures, bottom row eigenvalue corrections. Panel a is a bar chart of coefficient magnitudes for the high carrier mode ce fifteen at q equals ten, showing a tall carrier bar near zero point nine seven at index fifteen with rapidly shrinking sidebands at thirteen, seventeen, eleven and nineteen, a tight cluster. Panel b plots cluster half-width versus q for carriers three, seven and fifteen, with a dotted grey line at half-width two marking the capacity of a five-by-five sideband box, showing when each carrier exceeds it. Panel c is the analogous coefficient chart for the low carrier ce three at the same q, where the cluster has spread across all small modes. Panel d plots the eigenvalue correction delta versus q for ce fifteen computed three ways, with the five-by-five sideband (teal dashed) lying on top of the high-N reference (navy) and the three-by-three (coral dotted) slightly off. Panel e shows convergence of the truncated delta to the full value as sideband half-width grows from one to ten, reaching near machine precision by the five-by-five box. Panel f repeats the three-way comparison for ce three, where the five-by-five sideband is wildly wrong because the cluster has spread to the lowest mode.
fig21_3: Two side-by-side panels demonstrating singularity subtraction. The left panel plots Chebyshev coefficient magnitudes versus index n at N equals eighty on a log vertical scale: the naive expansion (coral) decays only algebraically, while the subtracted-singularity trick (teal) plunges to machine epsilon at modest n. The right panel plots maximum pointwise error versus N on log axes: the naive error stalls near six times ten to the power minus six even at N equals two hundred fifty-six, whereas the trick reaches about one point eight times ten to the power minus fifteen already at N equals sixteen, recovering roughly ten decimal digits.
fig21_4: Two side-by-side panels on cross-over truncation, both showing coefficient magnitude versus index n on a log vertical scale. The left panel is Boyd's cartoon: a straight exponential head ten times e to the power minus n over three (navy) and an algebraic tail ten to the power minus six over n to the fifth (coral), with their sum (purple) showing a clean slope change at a cross-over near n equals one hundred twenty. The right panel shows the real Chebyshev coefficients of a narrow Gaussian plus a weak endpoint singularity, exhibiting the same two-slope structure: geometric decay in the smooth bulk near the origin and slow algebraic decay in the far tail.
fig21_5: Two side-by-side panels for Schrodinger sech-squared scattering solved with a radiation basis. The left panel plots the reflection coefficient R versus wavenumber k on a log vertical scale, with numerical values (coral circles) lying on the closed-form curve (navy line) across about seven decades of magnitude. The right panel plots, versus k, the absolute error (navy squares) holding uniformly at the ten to the power minus eight to ten to the power minus nine level even where R itself shrinks to ten to the power minus eight, together with the asymptotic-constant drift, the magnitude of the sum of coefficients (teal triangles), which stays small because the potential decays exponentially.
fig21_6: Two side-by-side panels on Lanczos economization for an expensive determinant. The left panel plots the determinant D of lambda over the interval from zero point five to thirty, crossing zero at five roots, with the seventeen Chebyshev-extrema Lanczos sample points marked as teal dots; the colleague-matrix solve on the interpolant returns the root locations directly. The right panel is a cost comparison bar chart contrasting the naive scan-and-bisect strategy at two hundred ten expensive LU factorisations against Lanczos at seventeen, a roughly twelve-to-one saving, while both methods locate the roots to about ten to the power minus eleven accuracy.
fig21_7: A single semilog convergence plot of absolute root error versus the parameter N for finding the unique root pi over four of a given test function on minus one to one. The Ioakimidis non-iterative quotient (navy) drops geometrically, reaching about ten to the power minus twelve at N equals thirty, which is sixty-one function evaluations, while plain bisection using the same number of evaluations (coral) only reaches about ten to the power minus nine; the Ioakimidis result comes from a single quotient of two finite sums with no iteration.
fig21_8: Two side-by-side panels on the Hilbert transform via Fourier multiplier. The left panel plots the test function e to the power cosine x (navy) and its exact Hilbert transform (teal) against y over one period, with the FFT-based numerical transform at thirty-two Fourier modes shown as coral circles falling exactly on the exact curve. The right panel plots maximum error versus N on a semilog axis: the error plunges to ten to the power minus fifteen by N equals thirty-two and is bounded above by twice the modified Bessel coefficient (coral dashed), confirming super-geometric convergence on this analytic periodic test.
tbl21_2: A two-column table contrasting six precepts for the symbolic small-N regime against the usual large-N numerical advice, showing how each reverses (Galerkin versus collocation, Legendre or Gegenbauer versus Chebyshev, polynomialising and rationalising rather than leaving them, aggressive symmetry use, and basis recombination over boundary bordering), with the takeaway that working symbolically inverts the standard numerical defaults.
fig21_9: Two side-by-side panels for the Carrier-Pearson boundary-layer problem solved by four-term symbolic Galerkin. The left panel plots solutions at epsilon equal to one tenth and one twentieth against x, with the four-term Galerkin approximation (coral circles) tracking the exact cosh-layer profiles (navy). The right panel plots L-infinity error versus epsilon on log-log axes: the closed-form rational solution reaches about ten to the power minus nine error at epsilon equals one and grows monotonically worse as epsilon shrinks, because only four moments struggle to resolve the thinning boundary layer.
fig21_10: Two side-by-side panels for the symbolic quartic oscillator. The left panel plots the base-ten logarithm of the secular determinant magnitude over E from zero to fifty, where deep V-shaped dips mark the roots; a rug strip beneath marks the five Bender-Orszag reference values (teal circles) and the numerical roots in the window (coral crosses) for the five lowest even-parity eigenvalues, with the fifth root flagged by an annotated arrow as a mirage near E equals seven hundred twenty rather than stretching the axis. The right panel plots relative error per mode index: the lowest three modes are accurate to about zero point five, two point seven and six point nine percent, while the upper two are numerical mirages at one hundred forty-two and one thousand seven hundred ninety percent error, illustrating that only the lower spectrum is trustworthy.
fig21_11: Two side-by-side panels for the tau method on u prime plus u equals zero with u of minus one equals one. The left panel plots, versus N on a semilog scale, the amplitude of the Lanczos tau perturbation (navy circles) decaying geometrically to machine zero by N equals sixteen, alongside the pointwise error of the tau approximation (teal squares) and of a standard pseudospectral solution (coral triangles), both reaching machine epsilon by about N equals twelve. The right panel overlays the tau solution at N equals sixteen on the exact solution e to the power minus open paren x plus one close paren, the two being visually indistinguishable, with a residual perturbation of about five times ten to the power minus sixteen.
